newsitem.title: USA: American Eagle orders jets, sees moderate growth.
newsitem.headline: American Eagle orders jets, sees moderate growth.

text.p: American Eagle said Tuesday it ordered up to 117 regional passenger jets worth $2.4 billion in a move to allow the commuter airline to better feed passengers to its larger sister carrier, American Airlines.

American Eagle's move comes after an overhaul of its operations and the recent settlement of a bitter labour dispute with pilots at American Airlines over Eagle's plans to fly the new planes. Both carriers are owned by AMR Corp.
"That agreement paved the way for the introduction of the regional jets at American Eagle. It was clearly the stepping stone we needed to get here," American Eagle President Dan Garton said.
American Eagle announced orders for 25 70-seat regional jets from Bombardier of Canada worth $700 million and 42 50-seat aircraft from Embraer of Brazil, also worth $700 million.

The carrier also took options on another 25 of Bombardier's Canadair CRJ 700 aircraft and 25 of Embraer's EMB-145 jets, making the deal worth $2.4 billion, officials said at the Paris air show, where the orders were announced.
American Eagle will use the new jets to replace some of the 205 turboprop jets in its fleet and improve feeder service to American Airlines, the nation's second-largest carrier.

During contentious labour negotiations earlier this year, the pilots at American Airlines expressed concern that the new regional jets, which can fly farther than turboprops, would let American Eagle take some routes now flown by the main airline.
But Garton reiterated American Eagle's position that it does not plan to take over American Airlines' routes.

"The mission we're looking to pursue is to feed American's existing route structure better. It will not to replace to replace American flights. It will be to replace Eagle turboprops and, at some point" fly long, lightly travelled routes.
Garton said the regional jets may eventually provide service to cities such as Boise, Idaho, that "American simply can't and has not flown."

American Eagle said two-thirds of its fleet will remain turboprop jets even after the regional jets are acquired. The regional airline serves 127 cities in the United States, Canada and the Caribbean, connecting with American Airlines' main hubs.

American Eagle will accept delivery of the first regional jets next year and plans to start service in May 1998. The new jets will initially serve Dallas/Fort Worth and Chicago, where American Airlines competes against archrival United Airlines, the largest carrier in the United States.
"Certainly one of the most intense competitive pressures we have is to bolster American's hub in Chicago. Which is why we chose that first," Garton said.

American Eagle said it will replace turboprop jets with the larger regional jets, thereby boosting capacity out of Chicago. It did not say what cities would be served by the new jets but said it faced growing competition from rival carriers with regional service in Cincinnati, Cleveland and elsewhere.
"There will be some growth as a result of this acquisition," Garton said, noting about two-thirds of the regional carrier's customers connect with American flights.

Regional jets have become a contentious issue in the industry. Many airlines see regional jets as a less expensive way to compete with low-cost carriers. US Airways Group Inc., for example, recently said it was in talks to buy regional jets for its commuter subsidiaries.

United, a unit of UAL Corp., also wants to buy regional jets to feed its hub operations and add service to smaller markets. But United's pilots want to fly those jets rather than pilots at the United Express commuter airline system.
